statement: Sam tosses a coin three times and writes down H or T each time, in order, for example HTT. How many of the possible lists have more heads than tails?

choices.misconception: I counted only HHH, forgetting that two heads and one tail is also more heads.
I ignored the order, so HHT, HTH and THH counted as one list, plus HHH.
I counted only the lists with exactly two heads and forgot HHH.
I counted all the possible lists, not just those with more heads.

hints: A tree diagram splits into H and T at each toss, giving every possible list exactly once. Then pick out the lists where heads outnumber tails.
There are 8 lists. More heads means 3 heads, or 2 heads and 1 tail in any order.

solutions.reliable: A tree with two branches at each of three tosses gives 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 lists: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT. More heads than tails means at least 2 heads: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH. That is 4 lists. The transferable idea: a tree diagram lists every outcome once, so you can sort them without missing any.
solutions.elegant: Swap every H for T and every T for H. This pairs each list with more heads with one with more tails, and with three tosses there are no ties, so exactly half of the 8 lists, 4, have more heads.

whyOnTest: Tree diagrams make sure every ordered outcome is listed once, which is exactly what the order trap tests.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
